prompt: What does S3 store when the command line makes a presigned URL?
hint: A URL for a key that does not exist came out fine.

choices.text: Nothing; the URL is computed locally and checked only when used
choices.why: Right. Making it sends no request at all.

choices.text: A record of the link, deleted at expiry
choices.why: There is no list of issued links; S3 repeats the signature calculation on use.

choices.text: A public copy of the object
choices.why: The object stays private; the URL carries a permission, not a copy.

choices.text: The secret key, so that S3 can check the URL later
choices.why: S3 already knows the secret key of every key it issued; nothing is sent.

prompt: Match each parameter of a presigned URL to what it carries.
hint: One of them is why a pasted URL names a key.

pairs.right: The signer's access key id, the date, the region and the service
Seconds of validity after the signing moment
The signature made with the secret key

right_distractors: The addresses allowed to use the URL

prompt: A presigned URL valid for seven days leaked into a support ticket. What makes it stop working at once on AWS?
hint: S3 checks the signer when the URL is used.

choices.text: Deleting the ticket
choices.why: Anybody who copied the URL still has it; the ticket was only where it was seen.

choices.text: Deactivating the key that signed it, or removing the signer's access
choices.why: Right. The URL carries the signer's authority, which is checked at the moment of use.

choices.text: Making a new presigned URL for the same object, which replaces the old one
choices.why: URLs are independent; a new one does nothing to the old.

choices.text: Turning on Block Public Access for the bucket
choices.why: A presigned request is signed by the account's own key, so it is not public access.

prompt: In moto, a URL presigned for one second still works three seconds later. What should a test suite built on moto conclude about expiry?
hint: Who enforces the limit, and is it here?

choices.text: That clocks drift, and S3 also allows a grace period of a few seconds
choices.why: The lesson documents no grace period; moto served a URL with a broken signature as well.

choices.text: That the URL lives as long as the object exists
choices.why: On AWS it dies at `X-Amz-Expires` or with its credentials, whichever comes first.

choices.text: Nothing: moto skips the check, so test expiry elsewhere
choices.why: Right. Expiry is tested against the documentation or a real account; in this lab a presigned URL shows its shape and nothing about its safety.

choices.text: That one second was rounded up to a whole minute by moto's clock
choices.why: Nothing was rounded; the URL says `X-Amz-Expires=1`.

prompt: What is the longest `--expires-in`, in seconds, that S3 honours for a URL signed with an IAM user's long-term key?
hint: Seven days.

prompt: moto is started with `INITIAL_NO_AUTH_ACTION_COUNT=5`. What does the number mean?
hint: Count the setup.

choices.text: Five users may be created before IAM starts checking
choices.why: It counts requests, of any kind.

choices.text: The first five requests skip the IAM check
choices.why: Right. Every later one is checked; the five were the bucket, the report, the user, its policy and its key.

choices.text: A denied request is retried five times before failing
choices.why: moto does not retry; the command line retries server errors, not denials.

choices.text: Policies are re-read every five requests
choices.why: A policy takes effect on the next request after it is written.

prompt: The dashboard's policy allows `s3:GetObject` and `s3:ListBucket` and has no `Deny`. Why was its `PutObject` refused?
hint: What is the starting point of every evaluation?

choices.text: A bucket refuses writes from any key created after it
choices.why: Nothing about creation order matters; the policy is what is read.

choices.text: Because an action nothing allows is denied
choices.why: Right. The implicit deny is the default every policy starts from.

choices.text: `ListBucket` contains an implicit deny on writes
choices.why: An allow carries no deny; the write is refused because nothing allows it.

choices.text: The key had no permission because its secret was never printed
choices.why: Printing a secret changes nothing except who has seen it.

prompt: In moto's IAM mode, `aws s3 ls s3://quitanda-curated-prod` fails with `SignatureDoesNotMatch` and `--recursive` works. What is the cause?
hint: Compare the two query strings.

choices.text: The dashboard's key is wrong
choices.why: The same key signed the recursive listing, which worked.

choices.text: The policy does not allow listing with a delimiter
choices.why: A policy problem is `AccessDenied`, not a signature error.

choices.text: S3 refuses `delimiter=/` to IAM users
choices.why: S3 accepts it; moto is the one that fails.

choices.text: moto miscomputes the signature when a query value has a `/`
choices.why: Right. `--prefix reports` with no slash worked too. It is moto's defect, not S3's behaviour.

prompt: Why does the lesson read the new access key into variables instead of printing it?
hint: Where does a printed line end up?

choices.text: A secret on a screen ends up in history, recordings and screenshots
choices.why: Right. moto's keys are fake, and the habit is the one to keep with real ones.

choices.text: The command line refuses to print a secret key
choices.why: It prints it if asked; that is exactly what the `--query` avoids.

choices.text: moto would revoke a printed key
choices.why: Neither moto nor AWS can tell whether a key was printed.

choices.text: Variables keep the key valid for longer than a key that was printed on screen
choices.why: An access key has no expiry of its own; where it is kept changes nothing about that.

prompt: A bucket already has a public policy when `BlockPublicPolicy` is turned on, and `RestrictPublicBuckets` is left off. On AWS, can an anonymous request still read through that policy?
hint: One switch of each pair looks forward, the other looks back.

choices.text: No: `BlockPublicPolicy` deletes the public policy
choices.why: It refuses new public policies and deletes nothing.

choices.text: Yes, through the old policy
choices.why: Right. Only `RestrictPublicBuckets` neutralises a public policy already there; the blocking switches stop new grants.

choices.text: No: any one switch makes the bucket private
choices.why: Each switch does one thing; that is why all four are set together.

choices.text: Yes, but only for objects written after the switch
choices.why: The policy applies to every object it names, whenever written.

prompt: Why is the account-level Block Public Access the one the lesson calls most important?
hint: Think of a bucket nobody has created yet.

choices.text: It covers buckets created later, which nobody has configured
choices.why: Right. The stricter of account and bucket wins, so the account setting holds for the next bucket too.

choices.text: It is cheaper than setting it per bucket
choices.why: Neither is billed.

choices.text: A bucket-level setting cannot be read back
choices.why: `get-public-access-block` reads it back.

choices.text: The account setting is the only one moto enforces
choices.why: moto enforces neither.

prompt: With all four switches on in moto, which of these happened that AWS would have refused? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the transcripts after the switches were set.

choices.text: A bucket policy with `"Principal": "*"` and `Allow` was accepted
choices.why: Yes: `BlockPublicPolicy` refuses it on AWS.

choices.text: A `curl` with no credentials read an object
choices.why: Yes: `RestrictPublicBuckets` refuses it on AWS.

choices.text: A `public-read` ACL was accepted under `BucketOwnerEnforced`
choices.why: Yes: AWS answers `AccessControlListNotSupported`.

choices.text: `get-public-access-block` printed the four switches
choices.why: Reading the configuration back is what AWS does too.

prompt: A statement has `"Principal": "*"`, `"Effect": "Deny"` and a condition on `aws:SecureTransport`. Does it make the bucket public?
hint: Public access needs an effect that grants.

choices.text: Yes, because a `"Principal": "*"` anywhere in a bucket policy makes it public
choices.why: Only an `Allow` grants; this one applies a refusal to everybody.

choices.text: Yes, for requests made over TLS
choices.why: Not denying something is not allowing it.

choices.text: No: a Deny grants nothing; `*` says the refusal applies to everybody
choices.why: Right. Public access is `*` with `Allow`.

choices.text: Only if Block Public Access is off
choices.why: There is nothing public to block in it.

prompt: moto refused a read under a Deny conditioned on `aws:SecureTransport` being `"true"`, over plain HTTP. What does that show?
hint: On AWS that policy denies only TLS requests.

choices.text: That moto treats every HTTP request as TLS
choices.why: Then the policy with `"false"` would have let the read through, and it was refused too.

choices.text: That its denials prove nothing
choices.why: Right. moto does not evaluate the condition as S3 does, so a denial from it under a condition is no more evidence than a success.

choices.text: That the policy is wrong and would lock out Quitanda on AWS too
choices.why: On AWS, with `"true"`, plain HTTP requests are not denied.

choices.text: That a Deny on `s3:*` cannot be deleted
choices.why: The policy was deleted and the read came back.

prompt: What is the one check of whether an object is public that the lesson says to trust?
hint: Who signs the request?

choices.text: Reading the bucket policy carefully
choices.why: An ACL or another layer can grant what the policy does not show.

choices.text: A request from outside with no credentials, expecting 403
choices.why: Right. It tests every layer at once, the way a stranger would.

choices.text: `aws s3 ls` with the account's own keys
choices.why: The owner can read; that says nothing about strangers.

choices.text: `get-public-access-block` showing four `true`
choices.why: That reads a configuration; in moto it was set and enforced nothing.

prompt: The ACL group whose name sounded safe but meant any AWS account in the world was `___`.
hint: Not `AllUsers`.

prompt: Match each question to the AWS service that answers it.
hint: A door open, what is behind it, who walked through, and when it changed.

pairs.left: Which buckets are shared outside the organisation?
Who read this object last Tuesday?
Was this bucket's public access blocked yesterday and not today?

prompt: Order Quitanda's protections from the broadest net to the narrowest, as the lesson does.
hint: The account comes first, a single URL last.
items: Block Public Access on the account

prompt: A supplier with no AWS account must download one invoice this afternoon. Which is the safest way the lesson offers?
hint: Minutes, and the narrowest signer.

choices.text: A bucket policy allowing `"Principal": "*"` on that one key, removed tomorrow
choices.why: That is the first shape of a leak, and Block Public Access refuses it on AWS.

choices.text: A `public-read` ACL on the invoice
choices.why: ACLs are off under `BucketOwnerEnforced`, and a public object is public to everybody.

choices.text: A seven-day URL signed with an administrator's key
choices.why: Seven days and an administrator's authority are the widest, longest URL there is.

choices.text: A URL of a few minutes, signed by a role that reads only that prefix
choices.why: Right. A leak of it is worth one prefix, for minutes.

prompt: Which of these did moto get right in this lesson?
hint: One layer is evaluated, the others are stored.

choices.text: Serving `curl` an object under a public `Allow` policy
choices.why: Right. moto evaluates that kind of Allow, and that is S3's answer too when nothing blocks it.

choices.text: Refusing a presigned URL used after `X-Amz-Expires` had passed
choices.why: It served one used two seconds after expiry.

choices.text: Refusing a `public-read` ACL on a bucket set to `BucketOwnerEnforced`
choices.why: It accepted `public-read`.

choices.text: Reading `aws:SecureTransport` in a condition
choices.why: It refused under the reversed condition as well.
